title.en: Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport
Know why long-distance transport needs mass flow

say.en: A teak tree lifts hundreds of litres of water a day, tens of metres up, and sends sugar down to its roots, all without a heart. It begins at the scale of a single membrane. In this lesson: Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion and active transport.
Name uniport, symport and antiport.
Know why long-distance transport needs mass flow.

body.en: In simple diffusion, molecules move passively from higher to lower concentration, across the lipid bilayer if they are small or fat-soluble. In *facilitated diffusion*, channel or carrier proteins let polar molecules and ions cross down their gradient, with no ATP; the proteins are selective and can be saturated. In active transport, carrier proteins (pumps) use ATP to move substances against the gradient. Carriers may be uniports, symports or antiports. Over long distances diffusion is far too slow: plants use mass flow of whole solutions in the xylem and phloem.

problem.en: A root hair cell holds 20 times as much K⁺ as the soil water around it, and K⁺ uptake stops when a respiratory poison is added. What kind of transport is this, and why?

steps.en: K⁺ moves from low concentration (soil) to high (cell): against the gradient.
It stops when respiration (ATP supply) stops.
So it is active transport by a membrane pump.

points.en: Simple diffusion is passive and needs no protein; it is slow over long distances.
Facilitated diffusion uses selective, saturable proteins but no ATP.
Active transport uses ATP-driven pumps to move substances against the gradient.
